pool.label: C1
pool.builds_on: The paper’s observation that heterogeneous oxidation, linked to cast dendritic microstructures (PMC6513993::web::004 and PMC6513993::web::007), leads to defective oxide layer formation and higher oxidation rates.
pool.what_is_new: Rather than modifying the alloy’s composition, this hypothesis proposes a processing route (heat treatment) to tailor the microstructure of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr to improve its oxidation resistance – a strategy not previously explored for this alloy.

fields.hypothesis: A post-casting homogenization heat treatment aimed at refining the microstructure of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will reduce internal chemical segregation and thereby promote the formation of a more uniform, adherent oxide scale that limits oxygen ingress.
fields.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr in its as-cast state with coarse dendritic structures and compositional segregation between dendrite cores and interdendritic regions.
fields.intervention: Apply a rapid heat treatment (or homogenization anneal) designed to refine the grain size and reduce microsegregation, for example, a solutionizing treatment above the solidus temperature followed by rapid quenching.
fields.conditions: Heat treat samples prior to oxidation testing, then perform isothermal oxidation in flowing dry air at 1100 °C for durations up to 200 hours under conditions that replicate service loading environments.
fields.structural_mediator: A finer, more homogenized grain structure with diminished chemical heterogeneity at the micro-scale.
fields.mechanism: The as-cast microstructure in NV1 exhibited coarse dendrites leading to heterogeneous oxidation and locally varying diffusion paths (as observed by differences in OL, IOD, and IND growth in PMC6513993::web::004 and PMC6513993::web::007). By reducing dendrite size and chemical segregation through homogenization, the diffusion of oxygen and metal species will be more uniform across the surface, enabling the formation of a more continuous and defect‐free protective oxide scale. This microstructural refinement is expected to mitigate localized oxidation acceleration and reduce overall oxidation kinetics.
fields.predicted_outcome: A lower net oxidation mass gain and a more uniform oxide layer morphology relative to the untreated (as-cast) alloy, while tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength remain within acceptable ranges.
fields.baseline: The as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy showing non-uniform, heterogeneous oxidation with higher mass gains and localized oxide scale defects.
fields.boundary: Effective for oxidation durations up to 200 hours in air at 1100 °C and under testing conditions simulating high-temperature mechanical loading.
fields.uncertainty: The degree of improvement in oxide scale continuity and the quantitative effect on oxidation mass gain are uncertain and depend on the effectiveness of the homogenization; experimental optimization of heat treatment parameters may be required.

falsification_experiment.design: Process two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples: one retained in the as-cast state and the other subjected to the proposed homogenization heat treatment. Expose both sets to isothermal oxidation at 1100 °C for 200 hours in flowing dry air. Characterize microstructures (using SEM/EDS) in cross-section and measure oxidation mass gains via TGA.
measurements: Grain size and compositional uniformity (via SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not display a significantly more uniform and less defective oxide scale (and correspondingly lower mass gain) compared to the as-cast samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C2
pool.builds_on: The paper’s demonstration of the importance of elemental interactions and the need for further oxidation-protection strategies, with Y reactive element engineering extending a known high-temperature oxidation control mechanism to this refractory HEA.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis specifically applies a reactive element approach (Y doping) in the context of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr—a strategy not explored in the paper—to enhance the adhesion of the protective oxide layer without compromising the alloy’s solid-solution design.

fields.hypothesis: Add a minor reactive element—yttrium (Y) at around 0.5 atomic percent—to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr to enhance oxygen resistance by promoting the adhesion and continuity of the native oxide scale during high‐temperature exposure.
fields.material_initial_state: As‐cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr showing useful room‐temperature tensile ductility (8–16%) and adequate high‐temperature yield strength but insufficient oxidation resistance.
fields.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by doping with approximately 0.5 at% yttrium while keeping the remaining elements equiatomic.
fields.conditions: Exposure in air at temperatures of 800–1000 °C for durations on the order of 5 hours under tensile or compressive loading conditions typical of strain rates 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1. Mechanical testing should be performed at room temperature and elevated temperatures after exposure.
fields.structural_mediator: An ultrathin, continuous oxide scale that is enriched with Y at the oxide/alloy interface, leading to increased scale adhesion and reduced spallation.
fields.mechanism: Yttrium has a well‐documented reactive element effect in high-temperature alloys: even in very small amounts it tends to segregate to the oxide/alloy interface and improve the adherence of the growing oxide scale (whether HfO2, Ta2O5, or mixed oxides present in such refractory systems). This improved adhesion suppresses scale spallation and results in a slower oxidation rate while the overall bulk BCC solid solution and its solid-solution strengthening are essentially maintained.
fields.predicted_outcome: A reduction in oxidation weight gain and the formation of a more protective, adherent oxide layer after 5 h of air exposure at 800–1000 °C, with room- and high-temperature mechanical properties remaining within acceptable variance of the undoped alloy.
fields.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which develops a non-protective, rapidly growing oxide layer under similar conditions.
fields.boundary: The Y addition must remain at very low levels (~0.5 at%) to avoid unintended phase formation or embrittlement. The improvement is expected under continuous exposure up to about 1000 °C and short-to-moderate exposure times (~5 h).
fields.uncertainty: While the reactive element effect of Y is well established in other high-temperature alloys, its quantitative impact on the oxidation kinetics and the detailed scale composition in a BCC refractory high-entropy alloy is less certain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and another with 0.5 at% Y addition. Expose both sets to air at 900 °C for 5 hours. Post-exposure, use SEM/EDS and XRD to characterize the oxide scale (its thickness, continuity, and adherence) and perform tensile/compressive tests at room and elevated temperatures.
measurements: Oxide scale morphology and composition (SEM/EDS, XRD)
Yield strength and ductility from mechanical tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (e.g., similar oxide thickness/weight gain and evidence of scale spallation) or if the mechanical properties deteriorate beyond acceptable variances relative to the undoped alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C3
pool.builds_on: Building on the paper's recognition that oxidation protection is necessary and that the high-entropy alloy’s surface state can be engineered without altering the bulk solid solution, this approach leverages controlled oxidation kinetics to form a protective barrier.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a pre-oxidation processing step to deliberately generate a protective HfO2 layer, a strategy differing from compositional modifications or external coatings, tailored specifically for the oxidation-prone Hf-based HEA.

fields.hypothesis: Introduce a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment to deliberately form a thin, adherent HfO2-rich surface layer on equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, thereby enhancing oxygen resistance during subsequent high-temperature application.
fields.material_initial_state: Standard as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which lacks a pre-formed protective surface oxide and suffers from rapid oxidation in air at elevated temperatures.
fields.intervention: Perform a pre-oxidation heat treatment in an environment with a controlled, low oxygen partial pressure (e.g., a mixture of inert gas with a low partial pressure of O2) at a moderately high temperature (around 700–750 °C) for a short duration (e.g., 1–2 h) to generate a thin HfO2-rich surface scale.
fields.conditions: After pre-oxidation, the samples are exposed to air at 800–1000 °C for up to 5 h under strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1. Mechanical performances are evaluated post-exposure at both room and elevated temperatures.
fields.structural_mediator: A dense and adherent HfO2-rich surface scale that forms during the pre-oxidation treatment, acting as a barrier to further oxygen ingress during subsequent air exposure.
fields.mechanism: At controlled oxygen partial pressures and at a moderate temperature, the kinetics of oxidation allow the formation of a slow-growing, continuous HfO2 scale that is compact and well adhered to the substrate. By pre-forming this protective layer, subsequent oxidation in full air is significantly slowed since the barrier reduces further oxygen transport into the bulk alloy, while the underlying microstructure remains unaltered to maintain mechanical performance.
fields.predicted_outcome: The pre-oxidized samples are expected to show a markedly lower oxidation weight gain and thinner oxide scales compared to untreated samples after 5 h exposure at 900 °C, with mechanical properties (yield strength and ductility) retained at levels comparable to the as-cast condition.
fields.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr which, when exposed directly to air, forms a non-protective oxide scale with rapid oxygen penetration during high-temperature service.
fields.boundary: The pre-oxidation parameters must be optimized to form a protective layer without thick oxide buildup. This method is expected to work for exposures up to about 5 h and temperatures not exceeding roughly 1000 °C; beyond these, scale spallation or transformation could occur.
fields.uncertainty: The optimal pre-oxidation conditions (temperature, time, oxygen partial pressure) for forming an ideal HfO2 scale in this alloy are not precisely predictable from existing data and will require process optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two groups of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples. Subject one group to a pre-oxidation heat treatment at 725 °C in a controlled atmosphere (e.g., 5% O2 in inert gas) for 2 h, and then expose both groups to air at 900 °C for 5 h. Characterize the oxide layers via SEM/EDS and XRD, and perform mechanical tests on both groups.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and continuity (SEM/EDS, XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not exhibit a significant improvement in oxidation resistance (i.e., similar or higher weight gain and oxide scale degradation) or if any detrimental changes in mechanical performance are observed compared to the untreated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C4
pool.builds_on: The paper’s insights into the importance of alumina scale formation for oxidation protection (PMC6427440 series) combined with known benefits of surface modification techniques in high-temperature alloys.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a non-chemical, surface-specific modification (ion implantation) to enrich the alloy surface with Al, enabling protective oxidation without altering the bulk composition—an approach not previously applied to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.

fields.hypothesis: Use surface-modification by ion beam implantation to enrich the near-surface region of the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy with aluminum, thereby triggering rapid formation of a protective alumina scale during high-temperature exposure.
fields.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with homogeneous but non-oxidation-resistant surface composition.
fields.intervention: Perform low-energy aluminum ion implantation on the surface (depths on the order of hundreds of nanometers) of the cast alloy to create an Al-rich layer while leaving the bulk composition unchanged.
fields.conditions: Oxidation in air at 800 °C for durations ranging from 5 to 100 h, with subsequent mechanical testing at room temperature and 1000 °C (strain rates of 10^–4–10^–2 s^–1) to ensure bulk properties remain intact.
fields.structural_mediator: A nanometrically thin, aluminum-enriched surface layer that oxidizes preferentially to form a dense α‐Al2O3 scale.
fields.mechanism: Ion implantation increases the aluminum concentration in the top surface region without altering the bulk alloy’s microstructure. When exposed to oxygen at high temperature, this modified surface readily forms a continuous alumina layer that inhibits further oxygen diffusion into the underlying material. This mechanism is similar in principle to the surface treatments used in superalloy applications (see TXT::wikipedia::Nickel_aluminide::003), but is applied here using ion implantation.
fields.predicted_outcome: The ion-implanted samples are expected to display improved oxidation resistance (lower weight gain, thinner and more adherent oxide scales) while maintaining the original ductility and high-temperature yield strength of the equiatomic alloy.
fields.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr that suffers from rapid oxidation and pesting in air at 800 °C.
fields.boundary: The treatment effect is confined to the near-surface region (e.g., the top few hundred nanometers), ensuring that testing is focused on oxidation behavior and that high-temperature mechanical properties remain governed by the bulk.
fields.uncertainty: The optimal ion dose and implantation parameters (energy, time) that yield sufficient Al enrichment without causing surface damage or embrittlement are not yet precisely known.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples; treat half with aluminum ion implantation under defined conditions and leave half untreated. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 h (and extended durations up to 100 h). Characterize the surface oxide scale (using SEM/XRD/EDS) and evaluate the mechanical properties (tensile testing) of both groups.
measurements: Depth profiling of Al concentration (e.g., via SIMS)
Weight gain and oxide scale morphology
Mechanical property tests comparing ductility and yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ion-implanted samples do not form a significantly improved and adherent α‐Al2O3 scale with concomitant reduction in oxidation rates, or if their mechanical properties degrade due to surface damage, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C5
pool.builds_on: The well-known principle of forming protective, slow-growing oxide scales (such as alumina in stainless steels) combined with the high oxygen affinity of Hf in the high-entropy alloy system.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis adapts pre-oxidation surface engineering to an equiatomic high-entropy refractory alloy, aiming to generate a tailored HfO2-rich barrier without compromising the intrinsic mechanical performance, an approach not previously explored for this composition.

fields.hypothesis: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment in a low-oxygen partial pressure environment to form an ultrathin, coherent HfO2-rich surface scale on cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which will serve as a protective barrier during subsequent high-temperature exposure in air.
fields.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with acceptable room- and high-temperature mechanical properties but with poor inherent oxygen resistance.
fields.intervention: Subject the alloy to a pre-oxidation treatment (e.g., heating to ~600 °C for 1–2 hours) in a controlled atmosphere with low oxygen partial pressure (e.g., 1–5% O2 in inert gas) to deliberately form a thin HfO2-rich scale, followed by exposure to normal air at service temperature.
fields.conditions: Pre-oxidation at ~600 °C in a controlled atmosphere (1–5% O2) for 1–2 hours followed by service-like oxidation at 800 °C in air for 5–100 hours, with mechanical tests performed after treatment to verify property retention.
fields.structural_mediator: A continuous, ultrathin, and adherent HfO2-rich layer at the alloy surface, which acts to limit further oxygen diffusion into the bulk.
fields.mechanism: Hf, having a strong oxygen affinity, preferentially oxidizes to form HfO2. Under carefully controlled pre-oxidation conditions, a coherent and protective HfO2 layer can form. This oxide is known to be slow-growing and highly stable, mimicking passivation in stainless steels (TXT::wikipedia::Stainless_steel::028). The pre-formed scale will serve as a barrier against oxygen during subsequent high-temperature exposure, reducing pesting and oxidation kinetics.
fields.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in oxidation-induced weight gain and improved scale adherence (reduced spallation) during 800 °C exposure in air, with minimal impact on the bulk mechanical properties, provided the treatment forms only a thin surface layer.
fields.baseline: The untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, which develops a nonprotective, rapidly growing oxide scale under extended air exposure at high temperatures.
fields.boundary: The pre-oxidation must be optimized so that the resultant oxide scale is ultrathin (e.g., a few hundred nanometers) and does not adversely affect the overall ductility or strength; applicability is for oxidation at 800 °C over 5–100 hours.

fields.uncertainty: The uniform distribution and optimal concentration of the reactive additives (Y and Al) within the laser-alloyed layer may be challenging to control, and the magnitude of the improvement in oxidation resistance is subject to experimental tuning.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples: one undergoing the laser surface alloying with Y₂O₃/Al₂O₃ nanopowder treatment and one as an untreated control. Subject both groups to 800 °C air exposure for 5 h. Then, use cross-sectional microscopy (TEM/SEM) to assess oxide scale thickness and adhesion, measure weight gain, and execute tensile tests at room temperature and 1000 °C.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and adhesion quality (via SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the laser-alloyed samples do not demonstrate significantly improved oxide scale properties (thinner, more adherent layer, and reduced mass gain) without a detrimental effect on mechanical performance compared to untreated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C11
top3.builds_on: The paper’s description of oxidation mechanisms where continuous Al2O3 scales protect against rapid oxidation, and on established pack aluminizing practices known to improve oxidation behavior in superalloys.
top3.what_is_new: This approach uses a post-fabrication surface treatment rather than bulk alloying to improve oxidation resistance in equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, thus potentially preserving the inherent mechanical properties of the cast alloy.

fields.hypothesis: Apply a surface aluminizing treatment via pack cementation to form a pre-oxidized, Al-rich layer that promotes the development of a protective Al2O3 scale during high-temperature service.
fields.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr in its as-cast condition with no special surface modifications.
fields.intervention: Implement a pack cementation aluminizing process that deposits a thin (~5–10 μm) Al-rich surface layer on the as-cast alloy.
fields.conditions: The treatment is designed for subsequent oxidation in air at 800–1000 °C for durations between 5 h and 100 h, ensuring that the mechanical properties remain comparable to those of the untreated material.
fields.structural_mediator: An engineered surface layer that, upon exposure to air at high temperatures, oxidizes preferentially to form an adherent, continuous Al2O3 scale protecting the integrity of the underlying refractory HEA.
fields.mechanism: The pre-deposited Al-rich layer will experience selective oxidation, generating a protective Al2O3 scale that acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion. This method mimics the layered oxide structures evidenced in the plasma-sprayed AlCoCrFeNi coatings (as detailed in sections 3.2 and 4 of the paper) and utilizes established aluminizing techniques known from superalloy processing (TXT::wikipedia::Superalloy::012). By confining the Al addition to the surface, the bulk high-temperature strength and ductility should be preserved.
fields.predicted_outcome: A significant enhancement in oxidation resistance—evidenced by reduced oxide scale thickness and lower weight gain during oxidation tests—while retaining mechanical properties comparable to the untreated alloy.
fields.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which shows inadequate oxygen resistance and pesting under the same conditions.
fields.boundary: The effectiveness is expected under isothermal oxidation conditions at 800–1000 °C for up to 100 h. Too aggressive conditions (e.g., very high temperatures or cycling thermal loads) may still lead to scale spallation.
fields.uncertainty: While the formation of an Al2O3 scale is well established, the precise thickness control and long-term adhesion on this particular HEA substrate remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (a) as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and (b) samples subjected to pack cementation aluminizing. Expose both sets to air at 900 °C for 100 h. Use XRD and SEM/EDS to characterize the oxide scales and measure weight gain. Conduct room temperature and high-temperature tensile tests to compare mechanical performance.
measurements: XRD phase analysis of oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminized samples do not show a substantially more continuous and protective Al2O3 layer (with reduced weight gain) or if the mechanical properties degrade in comparison with the as-cast state, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C2
top3.builds_on: The paper’s demonstration of the importance of elemental interactions and the need for further oxidation-protection strategies, with Y reactive element engineering extending a known high-temperature oxidation control mechanism to this refractory HEA.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis specifically applies a reactive element approach (Y doping) in the context of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr—a strategy not explored in the paper—to enhance the adhesion of the protective oxide layer without compromising the alloy’s solid-solution design.

fields.hypothesis: Add a minor reactive element—yttrium (Y) at around 0.5 atomic percent—to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr to enhance oxygen resistance by promoting the adhesion and continuity of the native oxide scale during high‐temperature exposure.
fields.material_initial_state: As‐cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr showing useful room‐temperature tensile ductility (8–16%) and adequate high‐temperature yield strength but insufficient oxidation resistance.
fields.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by doping with approximately 0.5 at% yttrium while keeping the remaining elements equiatomic.
fields.conditions: Exposure in air at temperatures of 800–1000 °C for durations on the order of 5 hours under tensile or compressive loading conditions typical of strain rates 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1. Mechanical testing should be performed at room temperature and elevated temperatures after exposure.
fields.structural_mediator: An ultrathin, continuous oxide scale that is enriched with Y at the oxide/alloy interface, leading to increased scale adhesion and reduced spallation.
fields.mechanism: Yttrium has a well‐documented reactive element effect in high-temperature alloys: even in very small amounts it tends to segregate to the oxide/alloy interface and improve the adherence of the growing oxide scale (whether HfO2, Ta2O5, or mixed oxides present in such refractory systems). This improved adhesion suppresses scale spallation and results in a slower oxidation rate while the overall bulk BCC solid solution and its solid-solution strengthening are essentially maintained.
fields.predicted_outcome: A reduction in oxidation weight gain and the formation of a more protective, adherent oxide layer after 5 h of air exposure at 800–1000 °C, with room- and high-temperature mechanical properties remaining within acceptable variance of the undoped alloy.
fields.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which develops a non-protective, rapidly growing oxide layer under similar conditions.
fields.boundary: The Y addition must remain at very low levels (~0.5 at%) to avoid unintended phase formation or embrittlement. The improvement is expected under continuous exposure up to about 1000 °C and short-to-moderate exposure times (~5 h).
fields.uncertainty: While the reactive element effect of Y is well established in other high-temperature alloys, its quantitative impact on the oxidation kinetics and the detailed scale composition in a BCC refractory high-entropy alloy is less certain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and another with 0.5 at% Y addition. Expose both sets to air at 900 °C for 5 hours. Post-exposure, use SEM/EDS and XRD to characterize the oxide scale (its thickness, continuity, and adherence) and perform tensile/compressive tests at room and elevated temperatures.
measurements: Oxide scale morphology and composition (SEM/EDS, XRD)
Yield strength and ductility from mechanical tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (e.g., similar oxide thickness/weight gain and evidence of scale spallation) or if the mechanical properties deteriorate beyond acceptable variances relative to the undoped alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C6
top3.builds_on: This hypothesis builds on the previously reported concept of sputtered Al-rich coatings but improves it by tailoring the film composition (adding a small amount of Hf) to better match the substrate and improve interfacial bonding.
top3.what_is_new: It uniquely uses a composite Hf–Al sputtered film and controlled pre-oxidation to form a graded oxide scale that is specifically engineered to match the chemistry of HfNbTaTiZr, addressing the interfacial adhesion and thermal-expansion mismatch issues not discussed in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Tailor a sputtered, mixed Hf–Al surface film that in situ converts to an alumina‐rich scale with graded interfacial chemistry to improve adhesion.
fields.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr that shows acceptable room‐ and high‐temperature mechanical properties but develops rapidly oxidizing, spalling scales when exposed in air at 800–1200 °C.
fields.intervention: Deposit via magnetron sputtering a very thin (≈100 nm) film using a composite target of Al with a small fraction of Hf (e.g., 80/20 at.% Al/Hf) so that the film chemistry is partially matched to the substrate. Follow deposition with a short, controlled heat treatment (e.g., ramp to ~900 °C in a mildly oxidizing atmosphere such as 10–20% O2 in argon for 10 min) to convert the film into a dense, graded oxide scale.
fields.conditions: Post-treatment, samples are tested under isothermal oxidation in air at 800 °C and 1200 °C for durations up to 100 h. Standard mechanical tests (room-temperature tensile ductility and ~1000 °C yield strength at strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹) are performed.
fields.structural_mediator: A thin, graded surface scale composed primarily of Al2O3 embedded with minor Hf–Al oxide interlayers that gradually transition to the substrate, thus reducing thermal-expansion mismatch.
fields.mechanism: The mixed Hf–Al film is designed so that upon brief high-temperature exposure it converts to an alumina-rich oxide; the added Hf in the film helps tailor the interfacial chemistry and promotes chemical compatibility with the Hf-rich substrate. The graded interface alleviates mismatch stresses and leads to a continuous, adherent barrier that retards oxygen ingress.
fields.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to show a significantly lower oxidation mass gain (substantial reduction compared to untreated samples) with a smooth, non-spalling, protective oxide scale, while retaining its original mechanical properties.
fields.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr forms thick, rapidly growing oxide scales that spall during prolonged exposure in air at high temperatures.
fields.boundary: The process is applicable for oxidation environments in air at 800–1200 °C for exposure times up to 100 h; the film thickness must remain in the order of 100 nm to avoid altering the bulk alloy properties.
fields.uncertainty: The precise tuning of the Hf/Al ratio in the film required to optimize adhesion and scale stability on this complex alloy is moderately uncertain and requires parameter optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr specimens: one set receives the composite Hf–Al sputtered film followed by the controlled heat treatment, and the other set remains untreated. Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation in air at 800 °C and 1200 °C for up to 100 h.
measurements: Oxidation mass gain as a function of time
Oxide scale thickness, continuity, composition and adhesion (via SEM, XRD, and EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation mass gain and fail to produce a continuous, adherent oxide layer – or if their mechanical properties are degraded relative to the untreated control – the hypothesis is falsified.
